deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It is a printed page, not a Gauss manuscript: p. XVI of the historical preface of an 18th-century German textbook of arithmetic and algebra. The bundle name 'HB.Leiste' suggests Gauss's copy of Christian Leiste's 'Die Arithmetik und Algebra' (Wolfenbüttel, 1790); that identification is mine and is not confirmed by the page. The text continues the survey of the history of the calculus begun on p. XV. Its claims, in order:
(1) The English learned the calculus from abroad rather than from Newton.
(2) Jacob Bernoulli first presented it in a form that showed its value.
(3) Johann Bernoulli spread it in France and added the 'exponential calculus', Leibniz's term (Johann Bernoulli, 1697).
(4) L'Hôpital's 'Analyse des infiniment petits' (Paris, 1696, quarto) supplied a textbook. He dropped plans for an integral-calculus volume because Leibniz intended to write one himself.
(5) Manfredi met this need in 1707 ('De constructione aequationum differentialium primi gradus').
(6) Leibniz's other work is noted: the calculating machine, the dyadic (binary arithmetic), and his computation of the 'Interusurium' (discounting of future payments; cf. his 1683 'Meditatio juridico-mathematica de interusurio simplice'). The book cross-references its own §163 here.
(7) Euler (born Basel 1707, died 1783) is praised, including the Letters to a German Princess and the 'Vollständige Anleitung zur Algebra' (1770), dictated to a servant who was a tailor. A biographical notice in the Allgemeine Literatur-Zeitung no. 13, 1785, is cited.
(8) Modern scholars are declared outside the book's scope.
The page ends with the catchword 'Inhalt'.
The only handwritten trace is a double oblique stroke ('//') in the left margin. It sits beside the lines on Leibniz's calculating machine, dyadic, and interusurium (§163), presumably a reader's mark, possibly Gauss's, flagging the discounting topic.
For context only (my addition, not on the page): the interusurium problem asks for the present value of a sum a payable after n years at interest rate r. Under compound discounting, which Leibniz advocated, this is a/(1+r)^n. Under simple discounting it is a/(1+n r). A perpetual annuity of 1 per year then has present value sum_{k>=1} (1+r)^(-k) = 1/r.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.

Historiographical claims typical of the period are debatable. One is the remark that Jacob Bernoulli, rather than Leibniz, first made the calculus understandable. Another is the anecdote that l'Hôpital deferred his integral calculus to Leibniz. In fact Johann Bernoulli's integral-calculus lectures circulated in manuscript.
The anecdote that the priority verdict hastened Leibniz's death in 1716 is the author's hearsay ('man giebt vor', 'it is alleged').
